analysis.one_liner: Guarantees bondholders and Social Security trust funds get paid first when the debt limit binds.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 221-207 with every Democrat opposed, but the Senate never voted and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Treasury, if the federal debt hit its legal limit, to keep issuing new obligations to pay principal and interest on debt held by the public and on the Social Security trust funds — and to exempt those new obligations from the debt ceiling. Everyone and everything else the government owed would have had to wait on whatever cash came in. It passed the House on May 9, 2013, on a nearly straight party-line vote, and the Senate Finance Committee never took it up before Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.who_benefits: Holders of U.S. Treasury debt — banks, money-market funds, foreign governments including China, and wealthy investors — would have a statutory guarantee of being paid before anyone else during a debt-limit standoff. Social Security trust funds get protected too, but the bill's design keeps financial markets whole while all other federal obligations bear the impasse's costs.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Treasury to keep paying principal and interest on debt held by the public even when the debt ceiling has been reached, and exempts the new borrowing used to do so from the ceiling.
Protects obligations held by the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance and Disability Insurance trust funds, so Social Security's own holdings are paid ahead of other government debts.
Forbids using the new obligations to pay Members of Congress, a provision added by amendment before passage.
Requires weekly Treasury reports to the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees while the special borrowing authority is in use.

analysis.who_pays: Every other obligation of the federal government. If the debt limit bound and receipts fell short, payments to Medicare providers, active-duty troops, veterans' benefits, federal workers, contractors, states, and tax refund recipients would depend on whatever money was left after bondholders were paid first.

drawbacks.text: The bill guarantees payment only for debt held by the public and the Social Security trust funds; every other federal obligation — military pay, veterans' benefits, Medicare providers, contractors, federal salaries, tax refunds — would rank behind bondholders when cash runs short.

Rather than ending a debt-limit impasse, the bill leaves the debt ceiling in place while carving bondholders out from under it, so the fight over raising the limit would continue with the costs of the standoff shifted onto households and non-debt payees.

Critics in the House argued the bill put creditors — including foreign holders of U.S. debt — ahead of seniors and veterans; a Democratic motion to recommit that would have required the Secretary to protect seniors, veterans, and disaster victims instead of prioritizing all public debt failed 200-227.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — never missing a payment on the national debt — protects the one thing that would trigger a market crisis, and shielding Social Security trust funds is genuinely protective. But the design accomplishes it by standing creditors at the front of every line, leaving troops, seniors outside the trust-fund mechanism, providers, and contractors to absorb the consequences of a debt-limit standoff, and by letting the ceiling itself keep binding everything except the borrowing that services bondholders. It addresses the debt limit's cheapest symptom and hands the most expensive risks to people who have no say in the impasse.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 221-207 on May 9, 2013, but the Senate referred it to the Finance Committee, which never voted, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2013, as the government approached the debt limit, and was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
The Ways and Means Committee ordered it reported amended on April 24, 2013, by a 22-14 vote, and reported it on April 30.

On May 9, 2013, a Democratic motion to recommit — instructing the committee to add a section protecting seniors, veterans, and disaster victims rather than paying all public debt first — failed 200-227, with 198 of 201 Democrats in favor and only 2 of 227 Republicans.
The bill passed the House that same day 221-207: 221 of 231 voting Republicans in favor, 0 of 201 Democrats.
The Senate received the bill on May 13, 2013, and referred it to the Committee on Finance, where no further action ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Bondholders never got statutory priority. Seniors, troops, contractors, and every other federal payee kept their ordinary equal claim on the government's cash, and the Treasury kept full flexibility in any future debt-limit standoff.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seniors, troops, and contractors kept equal claim

industries.industry: Holders of U.S. Treasury debt (banks, money-market funds, foreign governments, wealthy investors)
industries.note: The bill would make them the first claim on federal cash during a debt-limit standoff, ahead of troops, seniors, providers, and contractors. Its gain is precisely the public's loss in a cash shortfall.

industries.industry: Federal contractors, Medicare providers, and other government payees
industries.note: They would rank behind bondholders whenever receipts ran short, absorbing delayed or missed payments during any impasse. Ordinary people who depend on the same payments would lose alongside them.

The bill shields obligations held by the OASI and DI trust funds, protecting Social Security's holdings. But it protects only those two trust funds — Medicare, veterans' programs, and other trust funds get no such guarantee.
